deep.reconstruction:
Setting (from §287): d = 2p+1 is an odd prime. In §288 Euler showed that the residues of 1^2, 2^2, ..., p^2 mod d are pairwise distinct. The reason is that a^2 ≡ b^2 forces d | (a-b)(a+b), and 0 < a+b < d.

§289. Euler tabulates the roots 1..p, the squares 1..p^2, and their least residues 1, α, β, γ, δ, ε, ..., π. There are exactly p distinct residues. In modern terms, the map a ↦ a^2 mod d on {1..p} is injective. Its image is the set QR of nonzero quadratic residues, so |QR| = p = (d-1)/2.

§290. The integers 1..2p are all coprime to d, so there are φ(d) = 2p of them. Exactly half are excluded from the residue list; Euler calls these non-residues and denotes them by German letters 𝔄, 𝔅, ℭ, 𝔇. Hence |QNR| = p.

§291. For any non-residue 𝔄, no square x^2 satisfies d | x^2 − 𝔄. So for each prime d there are exactly p 'indivisible' forms x^2 − 𝔄.

§292. The units mod d split into two equal classes, residues and non-residues.

§293. Closure of residues under multiplication. If m ≡ a^2 and n ≡ b^2, then mn ≡ (ab)^2, so mn (reduced mod d) is a residue.

§294. Corollary: if m and n are residues, then every power m^k and every product m^μ n^ν is a residue.

§§295–296. The residue set is a finite set of exactly p elements, yet it is closed under multiplication mod d. In modern terms, QR is a subgroup of index 2 in (Z/dZ)^*. Euler remarks that this is noteworthy.

§297. Take a residue m. All terms of the geometric progression 1, m, m^2, m^3, ... reduce mod d to quadratic residues; this is justified by §294.

§298 (finished on the next page). The powers of m can produce at most p distinct residues, since all of them lie in QR. Therefore m^p, or some lower power, is ≡ 1 mod d.

Pigeonhole step (my filling-in): among the p+1 powers m^0, ..., m^p, two coincide, say m^i ≡ m^j with i < j ≤ p. Since gcd(m, d) = 1, cancelling m^i gives m^{j−i} ≡ 1 with 1 ≤ j−i ≤ p.

The next page then confirms the stronger statement m^p ≡ 1 directly. From m = a^2 − k(2p+1) we get m^p ≡ a^{2p} ≡ 1 by Fermat. This is the residue half of Euler's criterion.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page.

§297 wording is loose. 'inter residua quoque omnia producta ex binis contineri' refers back to §§293–294 (closure under products), applied here to powers of m. The intended meaning — all powers of a residue are residues — is correct.

§298 as stated on this page only gives that some power m^k with k ≤ p is ≡ 1, not that m^p ≡ 1 itself. That needs either the divisibility of p by the order of m (not argued here) or the Fermat argument supplied on the next page. Euler's phrasing 'vel potestatem m^p, vel adhuc inferiorem' is accurate to what the pigeonhole argument gives.

results.what: Exactly (d−1)/2 nonzero quadratic residues mod an odd prime d, given by 1^2..p^2; the remaining (d−1)/2 units are non-residues.
results.modern_name: Count of quadratic residues modulo an odd prime
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (and earlier implicitly Fermat); standard since Euler's 1750s papers (E134, E242), later Legendre/Gauss

results.what: The product of two quadratic residues is a quadratic residue; the residues form a set of p elements closed under multiplication.
results.modern_name: QR is a subgroup of index 2 in (Z/pZ)^*
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Theoremata circa residua ex divisione quadratorum, E242, c.1760)

results.what: Powers of a residue m all lie in the residue class, hence by pigeonhole some m^k with k ≤ p is ≡ 1; in fact m^p ≡ 1 mod 2p+1.
results.modern_name: Euler's criterion (residue direction) / order of an element divides group order

deep.surprise_reason: This is the standard elementary theory of quadratic residues that Euler developed and published in the 1750s–1770s (E134, E242, E449). The Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792) is a well-known posthumous textbook presentation of the same material. Nothing here goes beyond what is already attributed to him.

checkable.sympy: all(len(set(pow(a,2,q) for a in range(1,(q-1)//2+1)))==(q-1)//2 for q in primerange(3,200))
checkable.asserts: Squares of 1..p give p distinct residues mod prime q=2p+1 (§§288–289).

checkable.sympy: all(set(pow(a,2,q) for a in range(1,(q-1)//2+1))==set(pow(a,2,q) for a in range(1,q)) for q in primerange(3,200))
checkable.asserts: Squares of 1..p already give all quadratic residues mod q (§§285–289).

checkable.sympy: all(all((m*n)%q in R for m in R for n in R) for q in primerange(3,100) for R in [set(pow(a,2,q) for a in range(1,q))])
checkable.asserts: The quadratic residues mod q are closed under multiplication (§§293–296).

checkable.sympy: all(all(pow(m,(q-1)//2,q)==1 for m in set(pow(a,2,q) for a in range(1,q))) for q in primerange(3,200))
checkable.asserts: For every residue m, m^p ≡ 1 mod 2p+1 (§298 and next page).

checkable.sympy: all(len([x for x in range(1,q) if legendre_symbol(x,q)==-1])==(q-1)//2 for q in primerange(3,200))
